newsitem.title: UK: Market players propose euro ground rules.
newsitem.headline: Market players propose euro ground rules.

text.p: Financial associations called on Thursday for European single currency policymakers to adopt a far-reaching set of proposals aimed at facilitating trade in the new euro.
The group has developed a new set of conventions on issues such as day count and decimals, to replace the current systems which will be swept away when the euro comes into being in January 1999.

"The joint statement...demonstrates the clear market consensus," the group said in a statement. "The associations are therefore calling on the EMI (European Monetary Institute), European Commission and all EU member states to support these standards."
The group includes international computerised clearing bank Cedel, Euroclear, the international clearing organisation and the International Swaps and Derivatives Association.

A lack of agreed guidelines on the basic nuts-and-bolt conventions for money markets, bond and foreign exchange markets has dogged preparations for the euro -- as trading houses are in the dark over how many days are in a bond year, and how forex rates will be quoted.
Computer systems will need to be developed and tested well before 1999, and this overhaul is being compounded by the need to change systems to counteract the so-called millennium bug.

"Economic and Monetary Union presents a number of technical challenges for the international and new domestic (euro-zone) financial markets," the statement said. "One of these is the need for market participants to be prepared for the market conventions that will apply to trading and settlement."

"Establishing harmonised euro market conventions will promote liquidity and transparency in the new markets, and prevent confusion and disputes for trading and settlement," the group said in a statement.
However, the group said that applying new harmonised conventions to existing, "legacy" instruments -- including bonds that redenominate into the euro -- present considerable complications.

In light of legal obstacles which could arise with revising existing conventions, and the dangers of mismatches if all contracts fail to switch, the group concluded that existing conventions should be retained for legacy instruments.

Among the recommendations for the euro money markets, it was proposed that euro business days and operating days for TARGET, the settlement system being developed for the new euro, should be identical.
This would mean that financial institutions unable to make payments on a particular euro day, because of a national bank holiday for example, would have to pay interest for the period of the delay.
The group recommended that bond prices should be quoted in decimals, rather than in the fractions used by the U.S. Treasuries and British gilts.

"Quotations in decimals provide for a more accurate and precise methodology of yield calculation, and will unify price quotation for government and corporate debt, as well as being easier for screen displays," the statement said.
